subtype: Testing the excuse [Response]

His numbers needed another week. The team would benefit from hearing someone new. He reread the email and asked himself: if his friend Rohit sent him this, would he buy it? He could hear his own reply: "You're nervous, yaar, just say so." Vishal deleted two paragraphs, then the third. The new message was one line: "Honestly, I'm nervous about presenting. Could we do a practice run first?" Usha answered in ten minutes; she had already booked the small conference room for Thursday. "Of course. 4 pm. 🙂"

Dear Parul,
Last week I sent you a long message about why I can't move into the flat with you: the commute, the rent split, my "need for a quiet workspace". This morning I did something odd. I wrote the real reason on the back of an electricity bill, and it came out in one sentence: I'm afraid that if we live together, you'll see how messy and moody I get, and you'll like me less.
Then I asked myself: if you had sent me my message, would I have believed it? No. You've known me since we were two girls sharing one lab stool, and your mother still calls me her second daughter. I'd have noticed the commute is twenty minutes, and I'd have called you.
So here is the shorter version, and it isn't flattering. I'm still not sure about moving in, but I'd rather decide it with you honestly than hide behind rent maths.
Can we talk on Sunday?
Love,
Vasudha

qa.a: On the back of an electricity bill.

qa.a: She feared that living together would show Parul how messy and moody she gets, and that Parul would like her less; the practical reasons felt safer to say.

qa.a: Admitting the one-sentence reason instead of repeating the rent maths, which gives Parul something real to answer so they can decide together.

qa.q: How might Parul feel reading this letter after the first long message?
qa.a: Parul may feel relieved and trusted, because the first message left her guessing, while this one shows a worry she can actually respond to.

In the school library, Sabina had three printouts spread across the table: kidney function, dialysis, survival rates for people over seventy. Bhupen sat down with his maths book. "Aren't you on leave this week?"

I've managed people for only three years, so I almost missed it. When Joseph was laid off from our team in March, he handled it better than I did. He wrote a clear handover document. He told me, "It's a budget decision, not a performance one. I understand the reasoning." He even helped me draft the announcement to the team. 14 August
Team-lead post announced today, and it's me. Ayesha, who applied for the same role, hugged me first. Then she told the whole floor, "She's the best choice, the best, honestly, I'd have picked her myself!" At lunch she said it again. In the lift she said it again, to the security guard. By evening she'd posted in the team chat: "SO deserved!!! 🎉"
Part of me felt celebrated. Part of me felt watched. It was too much, too often, and her jaw looked tight when she smiled.
But I also know Ayesha. She covered my shifts when Amma was in hospital. So I'm not going to decide she secretly hates me. Maybe she's happy and sad at the same time. I would be.
Tomorrow: ask her for coffee. Just the two of us. No promotion talk unless she brings it up.
Kavitha
